name: Peak-End Rule
description: People judge an experience mostly by how it felt at its most intense moment and at its end, not by its average or total.
design_relevance_note: Directly informs onboarding-flow design, checkout-completion moments, and error-recovery UX (make the ending good).
myth_risk_note: Miron-Shatz (10.1037/a0015295) found the rule does not hold for multi-episode retrospective evaluation of full days; duration-weighted average was a better predictor, suggesting the rule's domain is narrower than commonly claimed in practice.
prevalence_note: One of Kahneman's own concepts, extremely widely cited in experience-design and service-design writing via 'moment mapping' and end-of-journey emphasis.

findings.description: People's retrospective evaluation of a pleasurable experience is disproportionately shaped by its most intense (peak) moment and its ending, rather than by the experience's total duration or average intensity — extending Kahneman's originally pain-focused peak-end rule to positive experiences.
findings.source_title: Evaluations of pleasurable experiences: The peak-end rule

applications.title: Ann Taylor's exit-intent discount popup disrupting the end of a browsing session
applications.description: Ann Taylor's website displays a discount offer popup when a user's cursor movement signals they are about to leave the site, interrupting the natural end of the browsing experience with an unrequested offer rather than a clean close.
applications.ethical_note: This is an interruption/experience-quality critique, not a deception case -- the discount offered is presumably real, unlike the disputed pricing claims in the Amazon and Booking.com entries elsewhere in this corpus. Graded mixed because interrupting a user's intended exit with an unsolicited offer is a genuine, mild user-hostility pattern even when the offer itself is honest, distinguishing this from patterns with no user-experience cost at all.

applications.title: Duolingo's milestone celebrations reinforcing a positive peak during lessons
applications.description: Duolingo uses its cartoon mascot to celebrate user progress during lessons, including a distinct positive moment when a user answers ten questions correctly in a row -- creating a memorable positive peak partway through the experience, per the peak-end rule's account of how people judge an experience by its most intense point and its ending, not the average of every moment.
applications.ethical_note: Celebrating genuine progress accurately reflects something real the user achieved -- no inflation or fabricated urgency involved, a clean positive-reinforcement pattern. Contrasted directly against the Ann Taylor entry in this same wave, where a similar 'shape the ending' principle is used to interrupt a user's exit with a discount offer rather than genuinely improve their experience.
